title: Teaching Reproducible Research Using R
text:
About This Book
This book represents the applied companion to Reproducible Research Using R.
Over the course of the semester, students transformed structured assignments into fully reproducible analyses using real datasets, transparent workflows, and public-facing communication. What began as individual homework submissions evolved into polished research chapters assembled into this cohesive volume.
This book treats reproducibility not as an enhancement, but as a default professional practice.
Each chapter reflects a progression of skills: data import, cleaning, visualization, statistical testing, modeling, interpretation, and communication. More importantly, each chapter reflects a shift in mindset — from “running code” to designing complete analytical workflows.
This is not just a collection of assignments.
It is a curated portfolio of applied reproducible research.

title: Course Blueprint
text:
Course Philosophy
Semester: Fall 2025
Instructor: Christian A. Martinez
Institution: Brooklyn College, CUNY
This course is structured around a simple premise: reproducibility is not an advanced skill — it is a foundational habit.
Rather than treating R as a programming language to learn in isolation, this course approaches R as a complete research environment. Students learn how to move from raw data to interpretable results using transparent, inspectable, and reproducible workflows.
By the end of the semester, students do not just complete assignments — they produce a cohesive analytical portfolio.

title: 1  Assignment 1: Base R Foundations

1.1 Overview
This assignment introduces core concepts in base R, including arithmetic operations, object assignment, vectors, data frames, and built-in datasets. The goal is to build comfort with fundamental R syntax before moving into more advanced workflows.
You will complete all tasks in a single .R script.

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
2.1 Overview
This assignment continues our introduction to the Tidyverse using data from the pixarfilms package.
The pixarfilms package contains several datasets describing Pixar movies, including their genres, box-office performance, audience responses, and release information.
You will use these datasets to answer a series of questions about Pixar’s history and films.
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
2.2 Learning Objectives
By completing this assignment, you will be able to:

Use dplyr verbs such as select(), distinct(), mutate(), count(), group_by(), summarize(), and arrange() to explore data
Identify unique values within a dataset
Create new variables from existing variables
Use case_when() to recode categorical information
Identify the highest and lowest values using slice_max() and slice_min()
Calculate grouped summary statistics
Apply Tidyverse skills to a new dataset independently
Develop and answer your own data-driven question
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
3.1 1. Exploring Pixar Genres
The genres dataset contains the genres associated with each Pixar film. Notice that a movie can appear more than once because a single movie may belong to multiple genres.

3.1.1 1.1 What Genres Appear in Pixar Films?
First, let’s find out which genres appear in the dataset.
Using the genres dataset:

Use distinct() to identify the unique genres represented in Pixar films.
Determine the total number of distinct genres.
Arrange the unique genres alphabetically.

Question: How many distinct genres appear in the dataset?


3.1.2 1.2 How Many Genres Does Each Film Have?
Next, investigate how many genres are associated with each Pixar film.
Using the genres dataset:

Count the number of genres associated with each film.
Arrange the results from the greatest number of genres to the fewest.
Save the result as film_genres.

Question: Which Pixar film or films are associated with the greatest number of genres?
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
section: 3.2 2. Which Pixar Films Made the Most Money?
text:
3.2 2. Which Pixar Films Made the Most Money?
The box_office dataset contains information about the production budget and box-office performance of Pixar films.
For this assignment, we will estimate how much money a film made by subtracting its production budget from its worldwide box-office revenue.
Using box_office:

Use select() to keep only the following variables:

film
budget
box_office_worldwide

Use mutate() to create a new variable called net, calculated as:
worldwide box office - budget
Save the resulting dataset as pixar_money.
Using slice_max(), identify the three films with the highest net.
Using slice_min(), identify the three films with the lowest net.

Questions:

Which Pixar film had the highest estimated net?
Which Pixar film had the lowest estimated net?







Note



For this assignment, net is a simplified measure of financial performance. A film’s production budget and worldwide box-office revenue do not account for all costs or sources of revenue.
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
3.3 3. Turning cinema_score Grades into Numbers
The public_response dataset contains several measures of how Pixar films were received by critics and audiences.
One of these variables is cinema_score, which uses letter grades such as "A+", "A", "A-", and so on.
Let’s convert these letter grades into numeric scores.
Using the public_response dataset:

Use mutate() and case_when() to create a new variable called cinema_numeric.
Use the grading scale from our course syllabus to determine the numeric value associated with each letter grade.
Save the resulting dataset as pixar_scores.
Calculate the average numeric cinema_score across Pixar films.
Identify the three films with the highest numeric cinema_score.
Identify the three films with the lowest numeric cinema_score.

Questions:

What was the average numeric cinema_score for Pixar films?
Which films received the highest converted scores?
Which films received the lowest converted scores?
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
3.4 4. Pixar Through the Decades
The pixar_films dataset contains basic information about Pixar’s films, including their release dates and runtimes.
We want to investigate how Pixar’s films have changed across decades.

3.4.1 4.1 Create a Decade Variable
Using pixar_films, use mutate() to create a new variable called decade based on release_date.
Your categories should identify films as belonging to the:

1990s
2000s
2010s
2020s

Save the resulting dataset as pixar_decades.


3.4.2 4.2 Summarize Pixar Films by Decade
Next, group the films by decade and calculate:

Number of films
Mean runtime
Median runtime
Minimum runtime
Maximum runtime

Arrange the resulting table from the most recent decade to the oldest.
Save this summary as decade_summary.
Question: Based on your summary, do Pixar movies appear to have become longer, shorter, or stayed approximately the same length over time? Briefly explain your answer as a comment in your script.
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse
text:
3.5 5. Pixar Data Challenge
Now it’s your turn!
Using any dataset in the pixarfilms package, come up with one question about Pixar that you find interesting.
Some possibilities include questions about:

Box-office performance
Genres
Movie ratings
Academy Awards
Release dates
Runtime

You are not limited to these topics.
Write your question as a comment in your script.
Then:

Use at least three Tidyverse functions to investigate your question.
Show the code used to answer it.
Write 1–2 sentences as comments explaining what you found.
crumbs: 2  Assignment 2: Exploring Pixar with the Tidyverse

title: 3  Assignment 3: NYPD Shooting Incidents — Cleaning, Insights, and Visualization
text:
3.1 Overview
In this assignment, you will work with NYPD Shooting Incident Data using the nycOpenData package to practice data cleaning, feature engineering, exploratory insight generation, and data visualization with ggplot2.
Compared to previous assignments, this one is more open-ended: you will make a few analytic decisions (e.g., how to define time-of-day categories and which variables to explore for your second insight). This marks your transition from structured exercises to defensible analytic decision-making.

title: 4  Assignment 4: Merging Data and Comparing Means with t-tests
text:
8.1 1. Data Wrangling (Import + Merge)

Import both datasets into R:

Employee Info (Excel)
Employee Scores (CSV)

Notice the mismatch:

one dataset has First Name + Last Name
the other has a single Name column

Create a matching join key by doing one of the following:

Option A: split Name into first/last, or
Option B: unite first/last into a single full name
Clean the names: make sure all column names are lowercase and are connected through an _ (e.g. score_before)








TipWhen cleaning column names:



The clean_names() functio from the janitor can be very helpful.



Rename columns if needed so the join key matches in both datasets.
Merge the datasets so each employee has:

department
first name and last name (or full name)
Score Before and Score After

After merging, you should have 30 rows.

Write a short comment confirming the row count and what join you used.

title: 4  Assignment 4: Merging Data and Comparing Means with t-tests
text:
8.2 2. Handling Missing Data (Imputation)
Some Score Before or Score After values have been removed on purpose.

Calculate the average of each score column:

Score Before
Score After

Replace missing values in each column with that column’s average.

Tip: mean(..., na.rm = TRUE) and replace_na() (or base R) will be useful.

Write a comment confirming how many missing values were replaced in each column.

title: 4  Assignment 4: Merging Data and Comparing Means with t-tests
text:
8.4 4. Independent t-tests (Sex + Department)

8.4.1 4A. Add a Sex column (using babynames)

Add a Sex column by merging on first names using the babynames package.
If a name does not have an associated sex, remove it from the dataset.
Write a short comment reporting how many rows remain after this filtering step.



8.4.2 4B. Improvement t-test by Sex

Create a new column:

Improvement = score_after - score_before

Run an independent t-test comparing Improvement between male and female employees.
Report (as comments):

test statistic
p-value
interpretation




8.4.3 4C. Improvement analysis by Department
Using the same Improvement column, run a t-test in conjunction with the department column.
You can do this in one of two ways:

If department has two groups, run a standard independent t-test:

t.test(Improvement ~ department, data = ...)

If department has more than two groups, run multiple pairwise t-tests (or clearly explain why a t-test is not appropriate and what you would use instead).

Write a few sentences summarizing what you found.

15.3 3. Proposal-Style Structure
Your document should be structured as if it were an Open Data Week proposal.
Include the following sections:

15.3.1 A. Title & Event Description

A clear, compelling project title.
A 1–2 paragraph overview explaining:

Your research question
Why it matters
What attendees would learn


Write this as though it were submitted to Open Data Week.



15.3.2 B. Dataset(s) Used

Describe the dataset(s).
Provide proper citations and links.
Explain how the dataset(s) connect to your research question.




15.3.3 C. Analysis

Present a reproducible workflow from raw data to results.
Clearly explain:

What you cleaned and why
What transformations were performed
What analyses were conducted

Align every analysis step with your research question.




15.3.4 D. Visualizations
Include at least two clear, well-labeled figures or tables created in R.
All visualizations must:

Include titles
Include axis labels
Include captions
Be readable in a public-facing setting

Explain what each visualization shows and why it matters.



15.3.5 E. Audience & Relevance
Identify:

Who would care about this project?

New Yorkers?
Policymakers?
Journalists?
Community organizations?

Why does this research matter in a civic context?




15.3.6 F. Connection to Open Data
Explain how your project:

Demonstrates transparency
Highlights accessibility of public data
Shows the value of open civic information
Reflects open data principles
